# Human-Machine Shared Driving: Challenges and Future Directions

Shahzeb Ansari , Graduate Student Member, IEEE, Fazel Naghdy, and Haiping Du , Senior Member, IEEE

<small><span class="docvortex-page-footnote" data-block-type="page_footnote" style="color:#6b7280">Digital Object Identifier 10.1109/TIV.2022.3154426</span></small>

**Abstract— Distraction, misjudgement and driving mistakes can significantly affect a driver, resulting in an increased risk of accidents. There are diverse factors that can cause mistakes in driving such as unfamiliarity with the road, situation unawareness, fatigue, stress, and drowsiness. In emerging smart cars, sensing, actuation, advanced signal processing and machine learning are deployed to reduce the impact of driving errors by monitoring the state of the driver in real-time, detecting the mistakes, and deploying necessary actions to counteract them. Such strategies are collectively known as human-machine shared driving. Towards a better understanding of the developments taken place in this domain, as well as identifying gaps and trends in this discipline, a systematic review of the major studies and developments reported in the literature is conducted. The study is based on 155 papers of human-machine shared driving, selected through a thorough and comprehensive search of the literature. The review demonstrates that shared control approaches are mostly dependent on vehicle and environmental data obtained through various sensors. The majority of methods deploy active shared control by leveraging longitudinal and lateral dynamics. However, the precise recognition of driver’s intent and actions, accurate estimation of situation awareness, and modelling the trust between driver and automation are still major challenges preventing timely transition of control from the driver to machine or vice-versa, and resulting in fatal accidents. Major challenges in human-machine shared driving are identified and potential future directions of the work are explored.**

**Index Terms— Driving errors, influential factors, situation awareness, human-machine shared control, intelligent vehicles, trust modelling.**

## I. INTRODUCTION

D <sup>ESPITE</sup> the development and commercialization of smartcars, the rate of accidents has not significantly reduced as the deployed strategies and technologies do not address the major causes of fatal crashes, proved to be the driver distraction, misjudgements and mistakes [1], [2]. According to the Australian Road Deaths Database, of 4657 road accidents over the period from 2016 to 2020, more than 2000 deaths were caused by different driving mistakes [3].

Driver behaviour and styles have a significant impact on vehicle manoeuvrability, fuel consumption, steering system and pedals application [4]. Exact and reliable information on the driver state is necessary for active steering control and advanced driver assistance systems (ADAS) to provide safe and comfortable vehicle manoeuvrability. Knowing the drivers’ instincts and response to obstacles and collision avoidance are the challenges faced during dynamic state of steering and pedal movements [5]. Moreover, predicting the driver situational awareness levels, such as estimating high-level reasoning of the external scenes [6], interacting with multi-agents [7], predicting future events and behaviour [8], perceiving risks and identifying important driving agents [7], [9], are the key challenges faced by intelligent algorithms in real-time.

Generally, driver’s performance is affected by several factors, among which mental fatigue and drowsiness are the most serious [10]. Mental fatigue solely depends on the brain condition, resulting in tiredness, drowsiness, sleepiness and inactiveness. Moreover, the factors resulting in driving errors can be categorised as human or environmental factors [5]. As the result of human factors such as losing concentration due to fatigue and drowsiness [11]–[13] or aggressive driving [14], [15], driver can lose the control of the vehicle. The environmental factors can result in unexpected vehicle manoeuvres leading to frontal and lateral crashes in crowded traffic [16], or failure to control the vehicle due to unexpected road conditions and trajectory [17].

In the situations of driving errors due to distraction and misjudgements, the driver is distracted by secondary tasks, may miss the road path and end up in fatal accidents [1], [2]. A survey of 266 young drivers [18], showed that the most common distractive activities are using a cell phone, eating and drinking, navigating and talking with other passengers. In another study [19], it was shown that in 16556 vehicles, 24.1% of the drivers were engaged in distractive tasks under different roadway conditions. This is a serious concern as 35% of the engaged drivers were only involved in crossing roundabouts. Moreover, 57.1% of misjudgements occurred at intersections and 42.9% at marked pedestrian crossings [20]. Thus, engaging in distractive tasks while driving is the main reason for accidents. Therefore, it is critical that the driver’s errors are able to be accurately detected.

Numerous methods have been deployed to assist the driver by leveraging the vehicle performance and refocusing the driver on a predicted path by avoiding the obstacles and preventing collision [21]–[23]. However, these approaches only monitor and leverage the vehicle dynamics to compensate the mistakes and errors occurred during driving. In addition, the main problem faced in providing shared assistance is the transition of cooperative control authority, where virtual driver fails to take-over the authority and vice-versa as reported in [24], [25]. This happens due to unknown or erroneous estimation of driver states by the system, as well as poor modelling of trust between the driver and machine, that can ultimately fail to provide the required control action. Hence, a conflict between the control system and the driver leads to catastrophic situations. An increase in safety of the vehicle and reduction in risk of accidents can be achieved, if intelligent learning models and advanced controls are deployed to monitor the mistakes of the driver, accurately estimate the trust level of the driver on the machine, assist driving and even take-over driving if needed. This approach is known as human-machine shared driving.

The literature shows a growing number of scientific papers on real-time driving error monitoring and the shared assistance methodologies deployed to contract the errors. Towards a better understanding of the developments taken place in humanmachine shared driving, as well as identifying the gaps and trends in this discipline, a systematic review of the major studies and developments reported in the literature is conducted. This study has a two-fold aim, (1) evaluating the factors influencing the driving errors, and (2) identifying the methodologies developed to counteract the errors through intelligent human-machine shared driving technologies.

Towards such aim, the paper is designed to offer the following contributions:

\- A comprehensive review of the literature on driving error compensation through human-machine shared driving.

\- A critical study of the methods proposed and technologies used in detection of the driving errors.

\- Investigation of the state-of-art methods proposed and criteria deployed in human-machine shared driving control to tackle unreliable driving behaviour under different scenarios.

\- Identification of the gaps and challenges faced in the driverautomation cooperation during transition states.

\- Future work directions in real-time driving errors monitoring and deployment of intelligent human-machine shared control strategies.

More specifically, this study addresses a number of research questions and associated hypotheses as provided in Table I. The remainder of the paper is organized as follows: Section II describes the research strategy deployed in the study. Section III provides an analytical approach to the impact of driver behaviour on a vehicle, and the methods developed to detect driving errors. Section IV presents the critical examination of human-machine shared driving approaches proposed in literature. The future directions and conclusion are presented in Sections V and VI, respectively.

## II. STRATEGY

## A. Search Criteria

A systematic approach was pursued in this paper to identify the relevant and appropriate works during the search process. Initially, a general search was conducted based on IEEE and Scopus databases to gauge the status of intelligent transportation systems in the literature. As highlighted in Table II, a combination of various keywords relevant to the foci of the paper were used. The number of articles found in each database for the given keyword sets are provided in Table II. Approximately,

2049 journal and conference papers including book chapters, technical reports and lecture notes were found.

In order to refine the search, the lecture notes, chapters, theses, reports, and duplicate entries representing a lower significant original work were removed. The scope of the search was also restricted to English language journals and conference papers published between years 2000 and 2021. Fig. 1 shows the annual number of the journals and conference papers in the field of human-machine shared driving published from year 2000 to 2021 based on the keywords shown in Table II. In total, 238 scientific journals and 176 papers in conference proceedings with focus on driving errors monitoring were identified. There were also 146 journals and 157 conference papers published on human-machine shared control methods compensating driving errors. The bar graphs in Fig. 1 clearly shows a significant increase in the rate of publications in the area of human-machine shared driving from year 2013.

In order to further reduce the number of references and to identify the papers most relevant to the aims and objectives of the review process, a selection criteria based on Prisma Systematic Review criteria [26] was deployed, as shown in Fig. 2. The identified papers were filtered through following three stages:

![](data:image/jpeg;base64,)

Fig. 2. Prisma systematic review strategy.

Stage 1. Title scanning: The papers with titles not closely related to the field of human-machine shared driving for passenger cars were excluded.

Stage 2. Abstract scanning: The abstracts of the papers remained from stage 1 were reviewed, and the references that did not provide any scientific contribution to the research questions given in Table I were removed.

Stage 3. Full-text evaluation: The contents of the papers accepted in stage 2 were further evaluated and the papers that did not present any original contribution in detecting the driving errors under different factors and compensating for the errors through humanmachine shared control were excluded.

As a result, a total of 155 research papers were considered in the review process. Approximately, 76% of the selected papers were published in scientific journals, 17% in conference proceedings, and 7% were obtained from other sources such as webpages, arXIV repository, and statistical reports, as illustrated in Fig. 3(a). In terms of their foci as shown in Fig. 3(b), around 30% of the papers primarily contributed to monitoring and detection of different driving errors, 28% to identifying the causes of driving mistakes, 29% proposing strategies to compensate for the driving errors through lateral shared control methods (LaSC), 8% focused on longitudinal shared control methods (LoSC), and 6% contributing to shared authority control (SAC). It can be observed that papers in LaSC were mostly concerned with offsetting the mistakes made during driving. However, LoSC and SCA have not been thoroughly investigated in the literature. Furthermore, the search came across with only one review article on human-machine shared driving, though it dealt primarily with steering control algorithm used in different scenarios [27]. To the best of our knowledge, this work is the first review of human-shared driving strategies proposed to compensate the different driving errors.

## B. Structure of the Review

The review was structured according to the foci and the themes of the papers. Collectively, the 155 papers studied in the review covered two major areas of work:

a) Driving errors and methods developed to identify them.

b) Strategies proposed for human-machine shared driving to counteract the errors and mistakes.

The papers in category (a) addressed the factors contributing to different driving errors and the methodologies developed to detect them in real-time. On the other hand, studies in group (b) proposed strategies for shared longitudinal, lateral, and the degree of the authority control of the vehicle. This structure as well as the papers fitting into each group are illustrated in Fig. 4.

The category (a) papers could be further divided into two major groups, 1) papers on factors contributing to driving errors, and 2) the papers dealing with different types of driving errors. In the former category, there were papers studying human and environmental factors, whereas the papers in the latter group consisted of the works covering driving errors caused by distraction and the ones resulted by the driver misjudgements. The strategies proposed in category (b) could be further divided into three major groups, 1) LoSC, 2) LaSC, and 3) SAC. The papers associated with each group demonstrate the merits and demerits of different methods deployed to correct the driving errors through human-machine interface (HMI).

In the following sections, an analysis of the contributions by the selected papers will be conducted and the generic trends and directions of research in this area will be highlighted.

## III. IMPACT OF DRIVING BEHAVIOUR AND DRIVING STYLES ON VEHICLES

A number of studies reported in the literature examine driving behaviour and styles, and identify factors that influence driver steering/pedals actions and vehicle manoeuvrability [5]. Driving behaviour modelling can be classified into two groups. In the first group, the specific driving behaviour model is derived from a mathematical model developed based on a specific set of data [28], [29]. The mathematical driving behaviour is hardcoded based on threshold and rule-based strategies. Therefore, it cannot be used as a general driver model because it depends on a particular parametric relationship. In the second approach, known as learning based behavioural driver models [30], [31], the model is trained over large datasets to mimic human driving behaviour under different scenarios and conditions.

There are different categories of driving styles proposed in the literature [5], [32]. Generally, driving styles can be categorized as: 1) Aggressive style, 2) Moderate style, and 3) Defensive style. These driving styles can result in different mistakes during driving under various factors. For instance, an aggressive driving on a wet-skid windy road can be quite unsafe and result in under-steering or over-steering. Similarly, a conservative driver may become inattentive due to fatigue and drowsiness, resulting in unreliable manoeuvres and brakes under different road conditions. Such errors and mistakes directly affect the performance and stability of the vehicle and can end with a fatal accident. Thus, precise and accurate monitoring of the driver state and vehicle dynamics is necessary in order to prevent the dangerous situations. According to the reported studies, car following [28], [33], path tracking [34], [35], and double lane changing [36], [37] tests are commonly deployed to validate the proposed strategies and to classify a driving style in real-time.

In order to increase the driver safety and vehicle stability by detecting the driving errors and mistakes of different driver behaviours and provide shared control accordingly, it is important to understand first the different factors influencing the driving errors and the effective methods to identify them. These factors can be categorised as human factors and environmental factors. The driving errors could be caused by distraction and misjudgement, as depicted in Fig. 5.

## A. Factors Influencing Driving Behaviour

Driving behaviour generally depends on the driver current state, and dynamics of acceleration, braking, headway gap and cornering. In [38], driving behaviour was considered as speed and acceleration profile only. However, along with personality trait demographics, environmental factors, and external road conditions also influence driving behaviour [5]. The evaluation of the influential factors includes the type of factor, its effects, and the identification method. Fig. 5 shows the impact of different factors on the state of a driver and Table III lists the most common factors influencing driving behaviour.

The driving pattern mainly depends on driving conditions, driver intentions, driver actions, and vehicle dynamics. The drivers are usually distracted due to fatigue, stress and tiredness on a long trip [10], [12], [39]. Drowsiness can also cause the driver to perform unreliable manoeuvres [11]. Therefore, the driver’s lack of attention should be detected before the vehicle becomes unsafe and feedback should be provided to warn the driver. In this regard, the driver’s physiological analysis and visual features contribute to detection of drowsiness and fatigue characteristics [58]. For instance, the method proposed in [59] detects the driver’s reduced alertness by physiological measures based on heart rate, eye position and skin conductance.

Methods based on computer vision techniques are currently deployed to monitor the eye-lid position and mouth opening to detect the effects of yawning and sleepiness due to fatigue [13], [58]. Although, these techniques can be effective in detection, however, they have high chances of errors and false detection due to lighting conditions, use of sunglasses, and occlusion of part of the face such as covering the mouth by the hand during yawning. Moreover, methods based on physiological parameters such as Electroencephalogram (EEG), and Electrocardiogram (ECG) can be effective methods in a clinical environment but not feasible to be deployed during driving [60], [61]. Besides, drivers who are regular users of drugs and alcohol have higher risk of accidents [40], [41]. The Breath Alcohol Concentration (BAC) test is commonly utilized to measure the alcohol and drugs consumption level [40]–[42]. The work reported in [42] demonstrates the significance of steering behaviour under different BAC consumption levels. The research shows that the drivers tend to steer more when BAC levels are higher, leading to higher lane exceedances per kilometre on different curve radius. However, there is a research gap in the literature on real-time driver monitoring under the effects of alcohol, where systems should intelligently detect and classify the patterns. Many studies are focussed in understanding the driving patterns in a real-world scenario, where such patterns can be modelled efficiently for the classification of alcohol and drugs induced states.

In a questionnaire survey conducted in [62], [63], the driver behaviour is evaluated based on sensation seeking, driver anger, anxiety, risk perception and patience scales. The research showed that age and the factors described above have a strong influence on the driver behaviour and driving styles. The younger drivers with higher scores on sensation seeking and risks scales drive at higher risk compared to older drivers [14]. Technically such behaviour is reflected in higher speed, a lower headway gap and dynamic acceleration and braking [64]. In addition, instances of using mobile phones among the younger drivers is higher than older drivers, and 13% of accidents experienced by young females are due to distraction by cell phones [65]. Furthermore, in the pursuit of thrills and adventure, many young drivers drive carelessly, resulting in destabilisation of the vehicle and fatal accidents. More than 15% of young drivers are high adventure and thrill seekers, resulting in over-speeding and unreliable manoeuvrability [66].

Studies show that male drivers prefer to self-regulate their driving style on a long trip or during peak traffic conditions more than female drivers [15]. Self-regulating the driving style helps the driver to prevent critical situations and to increase awareness of the surrounding, which in turn enhances the decision making skill [43]. However, non-regulators, such as aggressive drivers, significantly affect the vehicle performance by sticking to a single driving style. For example, an aggressive driver may excessively accelerate the vehicle and makes it drift [44], [45]. Moreover, such aggressive behaviour can be dangerous on unfamiliar roads. As reported in [46], the unfamiliar routes require more concentration of the driver. Therefore, the aggressive driving behaviour should be monitored and regulated by an intelligent system to ensure driver safety and vehicle reliability.

Environmental factors also contribute to the driving pattern. Traffic signals and signs are for the driver’s safety and smooth transportation. Nevertheless, frequent signals and complex signs create irritation and ambiguity. It is shown that traffic violations mostly occur as a consequence of driver anger and distraction with secondary tasks [16]. Furthermore, the level of road complexity caused by lane variation and roundabouts can also significantly influence the driving behaviour [50]–[52]. Usually, the drivers tend to accelerate excessively on straight highways, violating the speed limit. Thus, results [17] show that low-sensation seekers possess patience, skill, ability, and suitably assess the demands of road complexities. On the contrary, thrill/adventure seekers are more prone to accidents.

In addition, rainy weather conditions make driving more challenging at high speeds because of variation in tyre friction causing the vehicle to skid and to roll [50]–[52]. Slippery roadways and reduced visibility can introduce complexities for drivers in selecting appropriate speeds and headway gaps [51], [53]. In this regard, non-linear observers help in determining the road variations through road friction and front tyres self-aligning torque information, as discussed in [48], [49]. Furthermore, it becomes more difficult to see pedestrians crossing roads at night. In a solution presented in [54], sudden motion of pedestrians is detected by deploying the far-infra-red cameras that monitor the temperature of the body in different weather conditions and seasons. However, the tracking becomes more challenging in severe lighting conditions. Lighting conditions can cause visibility problems and increase the risk of accidents in fog, haze and sandstorms [55], [56].

![](data:image/jpeg;base64,)

Fig. 6. Driver situation awareness cross-walk scenario: where two ego-vehicles are taking right turn at same time when pedestrians are crossing the road.

Driver situation awareness is an important hybrid (human and environmental) factor, which depends on external scenarios and motion of road-agents, and assists in challenging driving tasks. There are various scenarios involved where driver situation awareness and prediction are necessary, such as misjudging the speed of an oncoming vehicle during cross-walk when ego-vehicle intends to take right turn to merge on the perpendicular road as shown in Fig. 6. The road-agents such as parked cars on side roads, pedestrians walking on foot path, trees, cyclist, buildings, and surrounding vehicles are crucial parts of driver-road interaction [7], [9]. Hence, the driving requires critical scanning of external scenes, prediction of future behaviour of road agents, and appropriate allocation of attention to the situation to accomplish the driving tasks [8], [47]. In this regard, the intelligent systems monitor the driver’s visio-spatial skills through eye gaze tracking to estimate the driver’s attention [47]. Furthermore, driver’s visual features: 1) elapse time – time to encounter with object, 2) dwell time – a slight pause taken when becoming aware with the object, and 3) Gaze distance – distance between the eye gaze and object, are recorded and analysed to estimate the driver situation awareness in [6]. However, there are several challenges faced by the smart systems based on visual analysis in continuous monitoring the eye pupils for accurate gaze tracking, such as wearing sunglasses and inadequate lighting inside the vehicles that can prevent achieving this goal.

## B. Driving Errors Types and Detection

The mistakes and errors made by drivers are quite serious as they can result in fatal accidents. In New South Wales, Australia, almost, 14% of the car accidents are caused by misjudgement and distraction of the driver [67]. Hence, an intelligent monitor that can constantly monitor the driver’s state is required prior to the vehicle instability caused by the mistakes made by the driver. In this section, some of the most common mistakes and errors usually made by the human drivers are addressed and the methodologies proposed in the literature to identify those errors are covered. The human errors can be due to distraction caused by driver being involved in secondary tasks or misjudged actions resulting from wrong and inappropriate application of the pedals and steering wheel, as shown in Fig. 5. These error types are evaluated based on the metric of detection accuracy in conjunction with the assessment of deployed methods, and explored in Table IV.

The most common driver distraction is the usage of cell phones; particularly for calling and texting [68]. The study reported in [90] shows that 63% of drivers who participated in the study used cell phones for making and answering calls,

and around 59% of the young drivers between the ages of 16–20 years text while driving everyday [65]. The situation becomes more alarming when 40% of the participants reveal that they like to capture selfies using smart-phones while driving [90]. In [91], the Gaussian Mixture Model (GMM) was used to study the effects of texting under different conditions. According to the findings, in rainy conditions drivers have frequent lane and speed variations during texting. This is the riskiest situation that leads the drivers towards the fatal accident. In addition to highways and urban roads, drivers even engage in texting at railway crossings and, in some cases, drivers spend twice the time texting rather than concentrating on the road [92]. This increases the braking reaction time to the crossing warnings and reduces lateral position control. Therefore, it is important to detect the driver’s cell phone activity accurately while driving and to compensate for the errors through intelligent shared control systems.

A number of methods have been deployed to detect cell phone usage events. In [71], with an accuracy of over 80%, a Random Forest (RF) algorithm based on vehicle dynamics data is deployed to detect the texting behaviour of the driver. However, because of the limited accuracy and sensitivity of the RF algorithm, a Kernel Support Vector Machine (KSVM) is used in [69] to track calling (93.33%) and texting (86.67%) based on visual features. Further accuracy is achieved in [70] by utilizing Feed-forward Neural Network (FFNN) to detect the tasks of calling and texting. This achieved accuracies of 99.5% and 98.1%, respectively by training and testing with SHRP2 naturalistic driving study database. In this approach, the performance is evaluated based on the information of the vehicle speed, longitudinal and lateral acceleration, yaw rate and throttle position. However, detection itself is not enough as it is important to determine how much the driver is distracted. In [93], Euclidean distance (ED) regression analysis and Adaptive Neuro Fuzzy Inference System (ANFIS) machine learning predictors are deployed to detect the distraction, and a fuzzy logic algorithm is employed to identify the distraction level.

Drivers can also be distracted by eating and drinking while driving [68], [72]. With an accuracy of 81.26%, an RF algorithm is deployed in [71] to detect eating and drinking behaviour of the driver through vehicle dynamics. The detection accuracy is improved (up to 88.67%) in [69] using KSVM. Furthermore, by utilizing the Doppler Effect, the detection accuracy is increased up to 94.8% [73]. However, despite the high sensitivity, the generalization problem (such as, unidentified object interference and false reflection of objects) lacks the use of Doppler Effect approach.

Studies also show that the risk of accidents is increased when the driver is engaged in secondary tasks such as using navigation systems [74], and grasping an object [73], [81]. The work reported in [74] deploys a stochastic Wiener Process to model the effects of the navigation system on driver distraction. Furthermore, in [79], the heart rate and breathing signals are monitored to detect inattentive behaviour of drivers using non-linear autoregressive exogenous network (NARX). The physiological approach using health measures (heart rate, eye movements, skin conductance) is deployed in [59], where these measures are compared by EEG using different traditional machine learning algorithms and artificial neural network. These methods, however, require large experimental measurement efforts by electrodes attached on the human body and extensive signal processing and labelling. Nevertheless, these systematic studies can be helpful in understanding the nature of human driving that is needed in designing the intelligent vehicles. In another work reported in [73], the Doppler Effect method using a smart-phone speaker and microphone is utilized to identify driver inattention with an accuracy of 94.8%. The speaker transmits audio signals that reflect back to the microphone. Based on these signals, an early warning system intervenes by generating an audio signal to refocus the driver attention. However, because of unpredictable interferences of sound waves in the environment, the Doppler Effect lacks generalization and robustness.

In driving a vehicle, it is crucial for the driver to check the mirrors and perform head-checks while turning or changing lanes. In the study reported in [94], it is shown that engagement in secondary tasks can distract drivers from checking mirrors. The RUSBoost algorithm deployed, resulted in detection of the required mirror checking while changing lanes with an accuracy of 91%. Moreover, in order to track driver posture and motion during distraction, the driver’s 3D head and hands movements are monitored using FFNN at an accuracy of 82.4% [75]. FFNN is a powerful pattern recognition tool and is also applied in [70] to monitor the driver’s activity when engaged in conversation with passengers at an accuracy of 99.8% based on vehicle dynamics data.

Another category of driving errors is misjudgement such as underestimating the amount of steady-state cornering, wrong and sharp turning, speeding, and others as illustrated in Table IV. Generally, the methods deployed to estimate these quantities rely on vehicle dynamics data. In [84], the sudden manoeuvre of the vehicle at an intersection is monitored based on the information provided by a camera mounted on the vehicle along with the parameters of the vehicle dynamics using an RF algorithm. The study shows that maintaining a proper turn at high speeds in bends, slippery roads and snowy paths is more difficult. Hence, the driver may unintentionally under-steer or over-steer the vehicle and jeopardize the stability of the vehicle. Moreover, it is shown that fatigue and stress may increase the probability of over-steering 3.44 fold [95]. Therefore, in order to handle the critical under-steering and over-steering, an intelligent algorithm is deployed in [85] which measures the under-steering level based on the evaluation of yaw rate and lateral acceleration and comparing it against a reference trajectory model.

Driving conditions, such as at slippery roads and tyre pneumatic property are monitored in [86] based on tyre cornering stiffness co-efficient and tyre slip angle to detect under-steering, and to generate corresponding haptic torques at the steering wheel when the parameters cross a predefined threshold. On the other hand, over-steering is estimated based on steering angle, lateral acceleration, yaw rate and vehicle speed via fuzzy logic in [87], and compensation is provided through differential yaw braking when the over-steering level crosses the threshold. Another crucial mistake that can significantly increase the risk of accidents is speeding [4], [88], [96]. The study conducted in [4], efficiently classified the different speed profiles based on the vehicle longitudinal dynamics using a robust semi-supervised version of SVM.

The existing methods based on either vehicle dynamics or visual features, have both advantages and disadvantages. For example, visual features detect that the driver is distracted but vehicle seems running in stable manoeuvre in that particular moment. Similarly, through in-vehicle parameters approach the vehicle states are effectively identified but the method does not take into account the driver’s state that can lead to improper and unnecessary shared control intervention. Therefore, in order to have reliable and efficient shared control to handle the above driving errors, a combination of visual observations and vehicle parameters must be deployed to estimate the driving errors and to improve the vehicle stability through feedback of the error [97]. In addition, steering wheel hand positions should also be tracked to enhance the reliability of the intelligent vehicles under transient and steady-state cornering and variable speeds [83].

## IV. HUMAN-MACHINE SHARED DRIVING CONTROL

Different human-machine shared driving control approaches are reported in the literature such as, steering haptic feedback [34], [98], [99], shared steering torque control [100]–[104], lane departure and keeping system (LKS) [105]–[107], adaptive cruise control system (ACC) [108]–[110], fault-tolerant anti-lock braking system (FT-ABS) [111], and driver-automation shared transition authority allocation [24], [112]. According to Huang et al. [25], there are three types of automated controlled vehicle: 1) low-controlled vehicles based on surrounding sensors, where drivers possess full control authority, 2) LKS, ACC and FT-ABS lie in semi-controlled vehicles, where drivers intervene with the automated systems, 3) highly-controlled vehicles where controller behaves as a virtual driver and the control system has full authority to take-over the vehicle control when human driver fails to cope with difficult situations.

To assist different driving behaviour and to achieve a safe and comfortable driving experience in the presence of various driving errors under different influential factors, human-machine shared driving is an ideal approach. Such systems deploy an intelligent electronic controller that assists the driver by leveraging the vehicle outputs to provide the longitudinal as well as lateral shared control in path planning and collision avoidance. Furthermore, this system is needed for stable vehicle cornering at variable speeds under road variations caused by severe environmental factors discussed in Section III-A. It explicitly identifies the type of the driver that needs more assistance. For example, for novice drivers, the delay time and preview time are more than that for the experienced drivers in path following [21], [22]. Therefore, learner drivers need more assistance for comfortable driving under road variations. By applying shared control action, the vehicle becomes intelligent, active and driver fault-tolerant.

Generally, drivers are assisted through active and passive approaches. Passive approaches leverage the driving behaviour by providing haptic feedback through visual and audible devices [113]. On the other hand, active approaches directly intervene in the vehicle functions to overcome the driver deviation by leveraging the vehicle outputs adaptively [113]. This section mainly reviews the merits and demerits of active approaches and challenges faced during transition of control authority. The evaluation of human-machine shared approaches require efficient control of vehicle dynamics and predicting accurate trajectories in path planning. An overview of the fully automated shared control system is shown in Fig. 7.

## A. Longitudinal Shared Driving Control

Longitudinal shared control mainly depends on the leveraging of the vehicle longitudinal functions such as vehicle speed, acceleration and brake pedals positioning adjustment. This type of driving control has been commercialized in different form of control system, such as anti-lock braking system, adaptive cruise control system, as well as distance maintenance through speed controllers. A work reported in [114], deploys a reinforcement learning control strategy that controls the vehicle speed according to the environment sensing of the surrounding vehicles. The approach utilizes separate controllers for throttle and brake through Proportional-Derivative (PD) and Proportional-Integral (PI) controllers, respectively, to maintain a fixed distance to the preceding vehicle. Similar approach is also deployed in [115] based on game control strategies, where players (driver and controller) apply force on the pedal to maintain the fixed distance in a car-following case. However, the conflict between driver and controller control authority is the main issue faced due to unknown state of the driver and road variations. To overcome this issue, a driver-by-wire based co-operative shared control mechanism is deployed in a highway merging scenario by controlling the pedals position [116], [117]. The controller analyses the situation of the surrounding vehicles and provides haptic force-feedback at accelerator and brake pedals, respectively, according to control strategy shown in (1) and (2).

$$
\begin{array}{c} \alpha_ {i n} = \gamma . \alpha_ {c} + (1 - \gamma). \alpha_ {d r} \\ \gamma = \left\{ \begin{array}{l l} 0, & \alpha_ {d r} > \alpha_ {C} + \delta_ {l} \\ 1, & \alpha_ {d r} <   \alpha_ {C} - \delta_ {l} \end{array} \right. \\ F _ {b r k \_ i n} = \beta . F _ {b r k \_ C} + F _ {b r k \_ d r} \\ \beta = \left\{ \begin{array}{l l} 0, & \alpha_ {d r} > \delta_ {o} \\ 1, & o t h e r w i s e \end{array} \right. \end{array}\tag{1}
$$

(2)

here, $\alpha _ { i n }$ is the total acceleration of the shared system with $\alpha _ { C }$ and $\alpha _ { d r }$ as the controller and driver acceleration. $\gamma$ is the control authority co-efficient which is based on a predefined threshold $\delta _ { l }$ Similarly, $F _ { b r k \_ i n } , F _ { b r k \_ C }$ and $F _ { b r k \_ d r }$ are the total brake force, controller force and driver applied force, respectively, with the control authority dependent on the $\beta$ based on the predefined threshold $\delta _ { o } .$ In such approach, it is considered that the driver can override the system whenever the driver pedals application is greater than the threshold. However, this strategy is considered as binary approach, and the scenarios such as sharp curves, arcs and clothoid of roads require intermediate shared control action.

In another study conducted in [118], the problem of coping with traffic flow influence factor is addressed. The approach consists of a look-ahead cruise control system that controls the vehicle speed at an optimum value based on traffic data. The traffic data is obtained through online databases (such as Google maps, etc.) in which vehicle information is obtained through GPS function. However, the driving errors caused by the traffic when the driver unintentionally enters in the intersection and roundabouts are not yet considered. In this regard, adaptive shared control authority can provide efficient control to cope with such longitudinal driving errors using intelligent controllers.

Fig. 7. Fully automated shared control system.

## B. Lateral Shared Driving Control

Lateral shared control can be achieved by leveraging the steering wheel angle through haptic feedback torques, or a direct control system is produced by controlling the vehicle lateral and yaw dynamics such as direct yaw moment control system. This section discusses the different lateral shared control methods under different scenarios.

1) Path Tracking Scenario: In order to provide efficient shared access control in desired path tracking, the controller must initially predict the path accurately. Numerous techniques are proposed in the literature to predict the path [119]. At lower speeds $( v \leq 1 0   k m / h )$ , the kinematic model of path tracking is used as represented in (3), and at higher speeds, a following dynamic model is utilized [120], [121].

$$
\begin{array}{l} c \dot {x} = v (t). \cos \left(\vartheta (t) + \delta_ {r w} (t)\right) \\ \dot {y} = v (t). \sin \left(\vartheta (t) + \delta_ {r w} (t)\right) \\ \gamma = \frac {v (t)}{l _ {r}} \sin \delta_ {r w} \end{array}\tag{3}
$$

here, x and $y$ are the global reference frame co-ordinates with $v ( t ) , \vartheta ( t )$ and $\delta _ { r w } ( t )$ are the longitudinal velocity, yaw angle, and road wheel angle, respectively. The dynamic model, however, depends on multiple driver preview points as shown in Fig. 8. Multiple preview points help the vehicle to predict the accurate desired path of the driver. The co-ordinates of a preview point are predicted as follows [122].

![](data:image/jpeg;base64,)

Fig. 8. Multiple preview points [122].

$$
\begin{array}{r l} & D _ {l o o k} (t) = d + t _ {r e a c t} v (t) \\ & \quad x _ {p p} (t) = x _ {C G} (t) + D _ {l o o k} (t) \cos (\vartheta (t) + \delta_ {r w} (t)) \\ & \quad y _ {p p} (t) = y _ {C G} (t) + D _ {l o o k} (t) \sin (\vartheta (t) + \delta_ {r w} (t)) \end{array}\tag{4}
$$

(5)

In (4), the look ahead distance $D _ { l o o k } ( t )$ of the driver, which is dependable on the vehicle velocity, distance constant $d ,$ and driver reaction time $t _ { r e a c t } ,$ is defined. Hence, in addition to yaw angle and road wheel angle, the preview point $( x _ { p p } ( t ) , y _ { p p } ( t ) )$ depends on the position of the centre of gravity of the vehicle $( x _ { C G } ( t ) , y _ { C G } ( t ) )$ and $D _ { l o o k } ( t )$ as shown in (5).

In high speed cornering at sharp curves under external disturbances, mass and road variations, the driver fails to follow the desired path and loses control of vehicle. Therefore, vehicle state estimation is necessary for vehicle stabilization in path tracking. A method proposed in [123], deployed an Unscented Kalman Filter (UKF) for precise estimation of vehicle states and tyre-road friction. In another approach reported in [124], a Takagi-Sugeno Fuzzy model is utilised for path tracking to cope with mass and vehicle speed variations because of non-linearity of tyre and road friction. Furthermore, for more accurate estimation under parameter variance, Radial Basis Function Neural Network (RBFNN) can be utilized. An RBFNN can adaptively learn and estimate the uncertain tyre cornering stiffness co-efficient under different road conditions in tracking the desired path [125].

A number of methods are proposed to provide shared steering control in path tracking. One way is to provide haptics at the steering wheel [98], [126]. This approach is adopted in [34], where a haptic signal is generated through active steering torque at the steering wheel whenever the driver is diverted from the centreline. Moreover, it is also important to consider the neuromuscular response of the driver’s arm to monitor intention; whether the driver is inattentive or resisting the haptic torque induced at the steering wheel [99]. To predict this, a model predictive control (MPC) framework is utilized in [127], which predicts the neuromuscular torque response of the driver and provides haptics under inattentive driving behaviour.

Another method used to provide shared control is changing the steering angle ratio using steer-by-wire (SbW) system according to the driver’s desired path following characteristics for reducing the steering turning workload. In the work reported in [100], the steering ratio is tuned based on vehicle speed, steering angle, lateral position and yaw angle. To provide shared access under different driving behaviours, the steering ratio control strategy in (6) is used. This strategy adaptively leverages the steering angle which in turn varies the yaw rate gains defined as the ratio of yaw rate to steering angles [128]. Furthermore, recently using MPC framework, desired path is tracked by manipulating the front wheels of SbW system to track the reference-free trajectory [25], [129].

$$
\begin{array}{c} \aleph = \frac {G _ {r}}{K _ {r}} \\ G _ {r} = \frac {\gamma}{\delta_ {r w}} \\ K _ {r} = \frac {\gamma}{\delta_ {s w}} \end{array}\tag{6}
$$

where, ℵ represents the steering ratio, $G _ { r }$ is the ratio of yaw rate $\gamma$ to the road wheel angle $\delta _ { r w }$ , and $K _ { r }$ is the ratio of yaw rate $\gamma$ to the steering wheel angle $\delta _ { s w }$ . In another research conducted in [130], shared control is successfully achieved by putting the two players (Driver and Active Front Steering) in a closed loop information pattern using closed loop feedback Nash and Stackelberg equilibrium game control strategies and deploying the MPC to predict the vehicle states. Vehicle equilibrium is achieved by minimizing the cost function, constructed by comparing the driver steering angle and active front steering (AFS) predicted steering angle. The disturbance caused by the environment and road surface directly affects the front wheels in the shape of front wheel angle.

To develop a system robust to uncertain lateral disturbances, a zero sum game theory based regulator is designed with interactions between AFS and active rear steering (ARS) in the vehicle [131]. The shared control and stabilization are obtained jointly by two players through a closed-loop feedback Stackelberg game control theory to maintain the path tracking performance. Game control strategies are implemented in autonomous vehicles and can be utilized in systems to handle the steering authority over to the machine during unpredictable driving errors. Another method to provide shared access in path following is to utilize the vehicle lateral and yaw moment control method by controlling the yaw rate and lateral velocity simultaneously through independently actuated in-wheel motors [132]. The research conducted in [125], adaptively achieved lateral control stability by minimizing the lateral path tracking error using a back-stepping variable structure control method in a vehicle.

2) Lane Changing Scenario: In order to correct the driving errors while changing lanes and to comply with the traffic rules and regulations, the shared controller must detect the lane markers for precise lane departure. In the research conducted in [133], a driver assistance system is deployed to control the lane departure of the vehicle when drowsiness causes the driver to fail and comply. Lane departure in that system is predicted when deviation occurs with respect to the judgement lines, set at 0.5 m inside the lane markers on both sides of the vehicle. Furthermore, to improve the accuracy of detection of lane markers for accurate shared access, computer vision techniques have been utilized [134]–[137]. A piecewise linear stretching function (PLSF) is utilized in [137] which provided a detection accuracy of 97% under various lighting conditions. The algorithm improves the contrast level by segmenting the image region into two subregions using the Hough transform image processing.

To provide shared access control in avoiding the obstacles and collisions while changing lanes, particularly in the presence of preceding vehicles and surrounding stationary and moving objects, the controller should be aware of the driver’s intentions as well as of the intended path. In the study conducted in [138], the driver intention is detected based on vehicle lateral and longitudinal deviations that are compared with a predefined threshold, where the haptic torques are provided to prevent side collisions during lane departures. In another study, the driver lane changing intention is classified using a semi-supervised learning algorithm known as an inductive multi-label classification with unlabelled data (iMLCU) [89]. In this approach, the algorithm classifies three types of lane changing manoeuvres, namely, left lane change (LLC), right lane change (RLC), and lane keeping (LK) to avoid the obstacles in the lanes. The training of the algorithm is achieved offline based on the data collected of lateral offset and lateral velocity of the vehicle on a reference path.

Moreover, collision free lane changing tracking including an overtaking manoeuvre is achieved using convex optimization by Huang et al. [139] with MPC to predict the required steering and braking of a vehicle in an intended generated path. In contrast, the stability of the system is necessary while changing the lanes, as parametric uncertainties and driving behaviour variability degrade the vehicle performance [140]. To tackle the driving behaviour variability, a game-based shared steering torque control using feedback Nash and Stackelberg equilibrium strategies is deployed in single and double lane change manoeuvres [141]. The results show that during double lane change manoeuvres, the shared steering is co-operative. However, in single lane changing, the co-pilot develops a conflict between the human and controller because of single lane overtaking rules [142]. This issue can be resolved by emerging adaptive human-machine shared control in the system. Adaptive control is an effective tool to build the high performance controllers for poorly structured and time-variant processes.

3) Lane Keeping Scenario: To provide shared control in unwanted lane changing, a road departure avoidance (RDA) is designed using look-ahead distance approach [105]. The approach then leverages the steering wheel angle to correct the driver’s road departure to retain the vehicle inside the road curvature using $H _ { i n f }$ controller. The method monitors the lateral displacement of the vehicle and act accordingly to track the reference trajectory. Similar method is employed using fuzzy based sliding mode structure control to tackle the driver unstable steering movements through steering feedback torque and vehicle speed intervention [106]. Furthermore, the strategy is explored in terms of steering wheel safety envelope control in [143], where through steering haptic feedback torques the vehicle is restricted to retain inside the safety envelope (steering angle vs yaw angle and vs lateral offset). However, the driver-automation control authority issue remains in such approaches, where the controller overrules the driver. A co-operation oriented approach that minimizes the conflict between driver and control system is introduced in [144]. In such system, an adaptive shared control authority first monitors the driver activity through visual features analysis and then provides shared lateral control in the form of steering torques to retain the vehicle in the lane.

![](data:image/jpeg;base64,)

Fig. 9. Environmental envelope (Left) and Handling envelope (Right) [101].

4) Obstacle and Collision Avoidance Shared Control: In real time implementation of intelligent controllers, vehicle safety and reliable manoeuvrability can be achieved through shared control in the form of stability envelope control. The constraint based approach using MPC is designed to retain the vehicle in safe handling and environmental envelopes in [101], [103]. The handling envelope is constructed based on the information of vehicle yaw rate and side-slip angle. The environmental envelope is designed with boundary limits to ensure safe and collision free operation as shown in Fig. 9. The envelopes help in obstacle avoidance and collision control through human-machine shared control. The shared control is provided by adding extra steering torque in electric power steering systems, while in SbW systems the control can be achieved by incrementing steering wheel angle, required to bring the vehicle to a desired path through the feedback actuator [101], [103]. The study reported in [101], concludes that with predictive haptic feedback, the response time and reduced time to collision (TTC) are improved. The haptic feedback compares the driver’s steering angle with the predicted controller angle, and a reaction torque based on the difference is generated through a feedback motor in the SbW system. However, non-linear rear tyre saturation, which can cause over-steering, must be considered to maintain vehicle stability in a collision free environment. This problem is addressed in [102], and a successive linearization technique is deployed to model the effects of rear-tyre saturation. Simulation studies show that at high speed with a linear rear-tyre model, vehicle manoeuvrability as well as obstacle avoidance is achieved. However, in a real-world implementation non-linear rear-tyre model must be deployed for improved performance.

## C. Shared Cooperative Transition Control Authority

An advanced driver assistance system (ADAS) provides both passive and active switching of driving authority. In passive driving switching or passive transition control authority, driver presses the button to transfer the driving authority to the automatic system, such as co-pilot control or self-driving control, or vice-versa. Whereas in active switching control or active transition control intervention, the intelligent shared control system identifies the driving errors, and vehicle dynamics discussed in Section III, and adaptively intervenes to ensure stable vehicle operation and safety [145]. Hence, it can be stated that a shared control system is an integrated part of ADAS.

The active shared transition approach is deployed in [89], where a shared collision avoidance control is achieved using the Mamdani fuzzy inference algorithm by manipulating the control authority co-efficient (k) as defined in (7).

$$
U _ {s} = k U _ {c} + (1 - k) U _ {d r} \quad k \in [ 0, 1 ]\tag{7}
$$

where, $U _ { s } , U _ { c }$ and $U _ { d r }$ are the shared steering input, controller’s input, and driver’s input, respectively.

The co-efficient (k) decides the sharing authority based on TTC and lateral deviation index (η) according to the rule that lesser TTC and greater lateral deviation shift the steering control authority from the human driver to the controller to avoid the stationary and dynamic obstacles in an intended path. TTC is defined as the ratio of relative distance between vehicle and obstacle to the difference in velocities of vehicle and obstacle, whereas lateral deviation is defined as the ratio of change in lateral deviations to the upper threshold of lateral deviation, as provided in (8) and (9), respectively.

$$
T T C = \left\{ \begin{array}{l l} \frac {d}{v _ {h} (t) - v _ {o} (t)} , & \frac {d}{v _ {h} (t) - v _ {o} (t)} > 0 \\ + \infty , & \text {otherwise} \end{array} \right.\tag{8}
$$

$$
\eta = \left\{ \begin{array}{l l} \frac {\varepsilon}{2 y _ {l}}, & \varepsilon > 0 \\ 1, & \text {otherwise} \end{array} \right.\tag{9}
$$

where, d is the distance, and $v _ { h } ( t ) , \; v _ { o } ( t )$ are the velocities of the host vehicle and obstacle at time $t , \; \varepsilon$ is the change in lateral deviation between predicted path and planned path, and y<sub>l</sub> represents the upper threshold of lateral deviation.

Estimating the accurate value of (k) depends on trust (T) built between driver and machine. The trust can be defined as a sensorial model that enables the machine to estimate the reliance of driver on machine [146]. Modelling the (T) depends on driver’s observation $( \pi _ { n } , \varphi _ { n } )$ about the true or false hazards warnings $( L ( t _ { n } ) , F ( t _ { n } ) , M ( t _ { n } ) )$ issued by ADAS according to Fig. 10, and is given in (10) and (11) [147].

$$
T _ {(t _ {n} + 1)} = f (t _ {n}, T (t _ {n}), L (t _ {n}), F (t _ {n}), M (t _ {n}))\tag{10}
$$

$$
\left[ \begin{array}{c} \pi_ {(t _ {n})} \\ \varphi_ {(t _ {n})} \end{array} \right] = \left[ \begin{array}{c} g (t _ {n}, T (t _ {n}), L (t _ {n}), F (t _ {n}), M (t _ {n})) \\ h (t _ {n}, T (t _ {n}), L (t _ {n}), F (t _ {n}), M (t _ {n})) \end{array} \right]\tag{11}
$$

where, $f , g ,$ and h are non-linear functions at time $t _ { n }$ , with true warning $( L ( t _ { n } ) = 1 )$ , false warning $( F ( t _ { n } ) = 1 )$ , miss warning $( M ( t _ { n } ) = 1 ) .   \pi _ { ( t _ { n } ) }$ and $\varPhi ( t _ { n } )$ represent driver focus and ADAS intervention degree, respectively.

![](data:image/jpeg;base64,)

Fig. 10. Trust estimation framework [147].

Measuring the driver’s trust is a challenging task faced by intelligent systems, particularly precise estimation of driver’s observation $( \pi _ { n } , \varphi _ { n } )$ . In this regard, the work conducted in [146], deployed EEG system to estimate the trust of user on machine by reacting to the obstacles detected by machine are correct or incorrect. Research is currently ongoing to develop a practical approach to accurately estimate the driver’s trust for smooth transition of control authority.

The transition in active control authority needs to be stable. This issue is very challenging due to driver-automation interaction involvement. In [148], a shared steering control based on T-S fuzzy model in a LKS task is designed by monitoring a driver’s activity parameter known as fictive activity in conjunction with road-vehicle states. The simulation results demonstrate the effectiveness of the approach and correction of the driver’s lateral behaviour is achieved successfully based on predefined objective function of LKS. Furthermore, Han et al. proposed an adaptive steering torque framework to achieve the shared control resolution [149]. A dynamic driving load allocation based on Nash equilibrium game strategy was designed, where the steering torque of two players (human and automation) were compared. The dynamic transition allocation or control was achieved by sensing the steering torque of individual player. Explicitly, if the human driver applies more steering torque than machine then human driver can have more authority and vice-versa. However, it is challenging to allocate the authority to the respective player based solely on steering torque framework, as it is hard to judge which player or agent is driving correctly.

The switching of authority from driver to automatic system or vice-versa requires smooth transition. According to the literature, it has been observed that the shifting of control authority to the automation has been achieved successfully when the driver is diagnosed in an inattentive state [113]. However, under different circumstances such as in a crowded traffic environment, the automated system fails to complete the driving task. In addition, at certain conditions, where the capability of autonomous system is out of limit to cope with the driving conditions, switching of driving authority back to human driver becomes necessary. In such scenario, the main problem faced during execution is the conflict in authority transfer where machine imposes constraints to the human driver in handing over the control, possibly due to unawareness of the intentions and actions of automation (called “automation surprises”), when anomalies occur during timecritical situations [113], [145], or false detection and recognition of driver state by the automated system under various factors discussed in Section III-A.

To overcome this issue, Li et al. proposed an indirect active shared switching control authority by deploying SbW steering mechanism, where the driver’s steering angle command was first evaluated by the shared control system and then executed solely by the machine [150]. Hence, machine overpowers the human driver. This somehow resolves the conflict issue as driver can take-over the driving control by signalling the machine through driver steering command. However, poor surrounding scene understanding, sudden variations in driver behaviour, system malfunctions, and sensor faults can still contribute to authority conflict, where driver is restricted to gain the control.

Knowing the driver’s intent can overcome the conflict in active switching control mode [151]. The work reported in [152], deployed intention-based haptic guidance system that monitored the driver’s steering functions and through deep learning framework predicted the driver intention to cope with the lane-keeping and lane-changing tasks. Hence, the control authority degree (k) can be calculated according to (7) using weighted summation strategy. Many researchers are focused in proper modelling the dynamic driver behaviour under different scenarios and various influential factors, to achieve the precise and smooth shared transition or switching in control authority.

## D. Summary

An overall evaluation of the deployed and required shared control actions to compensate different driving errors are summarized in Table V. The need of required shared control actions are assessed to provide a research directions for the researchers. The requirement of the shared driving control for respective driving error is evaluated based on following criteria:

\- (+) if the required shared control is minimally needed.

\- (++) if the required shared assistance is moderately needed.

\- (+++) if the required shared driving is heavily needed.

## V. CHALLENGES AND FUTURE DIRECTIONS

Vehicle reliability and driver safety are crucial issues. Distraction and misjudgements are recognised as the causes of fatal accidents. The works reviewed demonstrate that fatigue, drowsiness, poor situation awareness, and road variations are the main factors that cause drivers to make mistakes. Moreover, shared steering and longitudinal control are deployed to correct the driver behaviour on pre-designed objective function (such as, path design, lane keeping, and collision avoidance) without knowing the exact state of driver leading to failure in transition of control authority. An analysis of the future work in this field to improve the detection methods and adopt intelligent controllers is conducted below.

## A. Surrounding Scene Understanding and Risk Estimation

To decrease the driver load and provide assistance, the in telligent vehicle utilizes various sensors and visual perception analysis to understand the external scenes and estimate the risks of moving obstacles. In this regard, the connected vehicle system (CVS) can provide assistance through wireless communication with the surrounding vehicles and ultimately can release warnings of road hazards to attract the attention of the driver to a critical situation [153]. However, driver’s dependability on CVS warnings could adversely affect dealing with other critical situations, such as when a non-CVS lead vehicle pulls to roadside for parking, or in a roundabout approach scenario when all other non-CVS vehicles from three sides arrive simultaneously. In such situations, no warning is issued by the CVS and the driver can unintentionally end up in a frontal accident during car following, or end up in a serious collision at the roundabout due to poor driver situation awareness.

To overcome the dependability issues occurred in CVS and to develop an independent external scenic perceptron and risk estimator, a simultaneous localization and mapping (SLAM) system can be deployed as discussed in [57]. The system utilizes a monocular and stereo camera integrated with inertial sensors to localize the motion of the obstacles and map the environmental scenarios, such as path planning. This is a robust system that regenerates the trackable maps in dynamic environment based on re-localization of key frames identified in planar and non-planar scenes. In another work reported in [7], the future trajectory of road-agents are forecasted based on past position information and action recognition by processing ecocentric views obtained through the camera in real-time. The proposed algorithms deploy multi-layer perceptron network to predict the future motion of ego-vehicle and other road-agents. Furthermore, a cross-modal trajectory prediction of road-agents based on hybrid system (LiDAR, camera, proximity sensors, radar) is proposed in [154]. Such systems are innovated to be implemented in autonomous vehicles. However, these systems require extensive exploration for deploying in shared-control system that can intelligently perceive the driver’s situation awareness by monitoring the HMI interface and vehicle dynamics, and comparing the trajectories of vehicle with predicted localization of road-agents, and deploy required shared control action accordingly as discussed in Table V.

## B. Trust Estimation Modelling

Modelling an accurate trust estimator is a challenging task. It is a time-dependent process where initially the machine needs to build up the trust collaboration with the driver for interval $[ t _ { n } , t _ { ( n + 1 ) } ]$ by providing precise active shared control through longitudinal and lateral intervention or by issuing warnings of oncoming and surrounding obstacles. Then it authorizes the shared driving system to assist in partial shared intervention or take-over the control during inactive state of driver. However, trust miscalibration such as under-trust or over-trust can lead to inaccurate execution of shared control action [155]. Therefore, it is important to model the driver’s trust relationship with the active shared control. In this regard, human behavioural responses are required by the intelligent system. Based on the literature, the responses are mainly acquired through subjective analysis, where the driver reacts to the questionnaires or recommendations made by the intelligent shared control as conducted in [155].

For objective estimation of driver response towards shared control provided in real-time, the intelligent systems should monitor the degree of driver’s resistance applied through steering torque on steering wheel in lateral shared control, or through pedal application in shared longitudinal control. The shared controllers can then compare the driver’s input applied through HMI and controller’s leveraging parameters in driving vehicle outputs (speed and steering). A relationship can then be modelled that will allow the intelligent systems to estimate the degree of driver trust on machine. Hence, such type of unique research opportunities will result in a more sophisticated and dynamic estimation of driver’s reaction objectively and indirectly through in-vehicle parameters and HMI.

## C. Real-Time Driving Errors Monitoring

To improve the detection strategy, driver behaviour must be recognized based on the combined framework of computer vision and in-vehicle parameters including the information of TTC with the obstacles. The intelligent detectors must be trained over hybrid complex parameters of vision and vehicle dynamics. The requirement of such approach signifies the improvement in detection accuracies of driving errors by monitoring the driver’s state visually as well as vehicle condition. An example of this approach is developed by MIT, known as Human-Centred autonomous vehicle [156]. However, the real-time implementation requires fast processors installed in cars. The core issues of early and fast detection in a real-time environment still need intensive experimentations and validations.

Another more effective approach is to monitor the movement and posture of the driver during driving using wearable sensors or motion capture system (MCS) [157]. The data in conjunction with in-vehicle parameters can be analysed using intelligent learning algorithms to detect mistakes made by the driver through driver posture analysis. This concept of monitoring the driver’s action using MCS is reported in [158], where driver’s pedal errors were monitored through right foot trajectory. However, this method is not feasible in practical real-time environment. However, analysing the driver behaviour based on posture analysis will contribute in specific monitoring of driver actions under different factors such as fatigue and drowsiness. Thus, MCS can help in identification of driver actions that will lead in designing of more improved smart and intelligent cars.

On the other hand, wearable devices, such as smart-watches, smart glasses, smart footwear and exercise wrist bands, are perceived as substitutions for physiological parameters in real-time driver monitoring. Ford Motors is also exploring the relationship between wearable technologies and driving, especially by applying the health monitoring features of smart-watches and fitness bands to vehicle technology [159].

## D. Potential of Deep Learning

Among the methods described in Section III-B for detecting driving errors by monitoring the driver state, Semi-SVM and ANFIS are the most suitable identifiers because of their robustness, generalization and adaptive learning efficiency. However, when dealing with larger datasets and complex information, these algorithms lack fast convergence and optimization. Even the feed-forward neural network lacks in classification accuracy, validation and testing due to unavailability of feedback memory element in sequence learning. Deep learning methods, such as multiple features detection from complex and non-linear data, are superior in performance compared to traditional machine learning approaches [160]. Convolutional neural networks (CNN) and Long Short Term Memory (LSTM) are the most recent advancements in the domain that learn using raw data instead of statistical features and provide fast convergence, great detection accuracy to cope with false positive issue. One such implementation based on multi-modal fusion model of CNN-LSTM is deployed in [161] where driver’s stress level classification is achieved. Therefore, by deploying such intelligence the accurate classification of driving errors under various factors and system constraints can be obtained. However, deep learning methods require large datasets for training and computational time as well as costs. Moreover, the problem of simultaneous operation of multiple system (intelligent detectors + shared controllers) running in real-time must be kept in account. The question still remains whether multiple systems will work reliably in a real-world driving smart car? These issues in real-time implementation still remain and require extensive exploration.

## E. Adaptive Human-Machine Shared Control

It was shown that most of the reviewed methods were dependent on the deployment of conventional steering and longitudinal systems to identify the impact of driver behaviour. However, mechanical steering systems require periodic maintenance and can provide wrong information that is a consequence of steering misalignment and wear-out of the components. A SbW system that is a type of X-by-Wire (XbW) system, however, is an effective tool to deal with these restrictions because of its simple structure and superior performance.

Most of the reviewed methods for shared control approaches are dependent on steering wheel control authority, however longitudinal control authority is neglected. Since, the driver under the influence of fatigue and road variations generally performs unreliable manoeuvrability as well as inappropriate pedal application. Therefore, to improve the driver safety and vehicle reliability both lateral and longitudinal shared control must be deployed. In addition, different driving behaviours can cause different errors that directly affect the performance and stability of the vehicle in path tracking and collision avoidance. Therefore, the consequences of such influences and distractions emphasize the need for a precise control action to prevent the critical situations.

A robust and adaptive human-machine shared control system can bridge this gap through learned driver model under different factors. The shared control can be provided adaptively by leveraging the steering wheel angle, artificial steering torque and braking for stable vehicle cornering in path tracking and collision avoidance. Even in the worst-case scenario, when drivers perform unreliable and unsafe manoeuvres or are entirely distracted by secondary tasks at high speed, the steering and longitudinal control authority can be transferred to the controller. The adaptive shared controller can then control the steering wheel and braking of the vehicle to avoid the obstacles and track the desired path. However, the control authority factor should be adaptive according to driver’s condition for the smooth and reliable transition of control when the driver desires to take back the control or the system fails to execute the driving task. Through deployment of adaptive and robust shared strategies, the vehicle can become intelligent, active and fault-tolerant to survive despite driving mistakes. To achieve this goal, innovative control methods should be formulated to support the application of adaptive shared control using XbW system under multiple systems constraint through analytical approaches rather than the deployment of separate controllers. The driver behaviour and styles can be identified efficiently, and accurate shared control can be provided in order to ensure safe and reliable manoeuvrability under different conditions.

## VI. CONCLUSION

The impact of driver behaviour and driving errors on vehicle under different conditions was explored in this paper. Through a review of the literature in this area, it was shown that major fatal accidents are caused when the driver is distracted by factors such as cell phones and eating, poor situation awareness, speeding and unreliable manoeuvres. Furthermore, active shared control methods proposed for longitudinal and lateral interventions were reviewed. It was observed that the deployed shared control approaches were dependent on vehicle dynamics and sensors providing information of surrounding vehicles. The proposed strategies deploy haptic shared control by leveraging the longitudinal and lateral dynamics during interaction between the driver and automatic system based on pre-designed objective functions such as path design, lane keeping and collision avoidance. However, exact recognition of driver’s intent and state, and estimation of driver trust on automatic systems, are still major issues yet to be addressed, where transition of control authority fails, resulting in serious situations. Algorithms based on deep learning methods have potential to address some of these outstanding problems. There is also a potential to deploy a hybrid approach based on computer vision and vehicle dynamics to develop more accurate system to assess the driver’s state. The paper also presented the significance of the future research in detection of driver actions through combined approach of wearable sensors and vehicle dynamics. Finally, the paper highlighted the importance of deploying adaptive human-machine shared control system in intelligent vehicles in compensating driving errors.

Shahzeb Ansari (Graduate Student Member, IEEE) was born in Pakistan. He received the bachelor’s and master’s degrees in electronic engineering in 2013 and 2017, respectively. He is currently working toward the Ph.D. degree with the School of Electrical, Computer and Telecommunications Engineering, University of Wollongong (UOW), Wollongong, NSW, Australia, under the joint scholarship of UOW Australia, and HEC Pakistan. His research interests include implementation of the intelligent learning algorithms in detection of driving behaviour

and human-machine shared access control. He is an active Researcher and contributor in scientific community, and has authored or coauthored in various journals and presented his work in IEEE flagship conferences. He is also an active Reviewer of IEEE TRANSACTIONS ON INTELLIGENT TRANSPORTATION SYSTEMS, IEEE TRANSACTIONS ON INDUSTRIAL INFORMATICS, and IEEE FLAG-SHIP CONFERENCE ON SYSTEMS, MAN, AND CYBERNETICS.

![](data:image/jpeg;base64,)

**Fazel Naghdy** was born in Tehran, Iran. He received the first degree from Tehran University, Tehran, Iran, in 1976, and the M.Sc. and Ph.D. degrees from the Postgraduate School of Control Engineering, University of Bradford, Bradford, U.K., in 1979 and 1982 respectively. He is currently a Professor of robotics and intelligent systems with the University of Wollongong, Wollongong, NSW, Australia, and the Director of Centre for Intelligent Mechatronics Research, University of Wollongong. He has a demonstrated track record and leadership in research, teaching, and management. He has more than 400 publications in international journals and conferences and as book chapters. His research interests include machine intelligence and control particularly in embedded mechatronics and robotics systems. His current research interests include haptic rendered virtual manipulation of clinical and mechanical systems, intelligent control, and learning in non-linear and non-structured systems. He is also a contributing reviewer of IEEE TRANSACTIONS ON MECHATRONICS ENGINEERING and International Journal of Intelligent Automation and Soft Computing. He has served on a large number of International scientific committee of various international conferences.

![](data:image/jpeg;base64,)

**Haiping Du** (Senior Member, IEEE) received the Ph.D. degree in mechanical design and theory from Shanghai Jiao Tong University, Shanghai, China, in 2002. He is currently a Senior Professor with the University of Wollongong, Wollongong, NSW, Australia. From 2005 to 2009, he was a Research Fellow with the University of Technology Sydney, Ultimo, NSW, Australia. From 2004 to 2005, he was a Postdoctoral Research Associate with Imperial College London, London, U.K., and with the University of Hong Kong, Hong Kong, from 2002 to 2003. His research interests include vibration control, vehicle dynamics and control systems, robust control theory and engineering applications, electric vehicles, robotics and automation, and smart materials and structures. He was the recipient of the Australian Endeavour Research Fellowship in 2012. He is a Subject Editor of the Journal of Franklin Institute, an Associate Editor for the IEEE TRANSACTIONS ON IN-DUSTRIAL ELECTRONICS, IMechE Journal of Systems and Control Engineering, and IEEE Control Systems Society Conference, an Editorial Board Member of Journal of Sound and Vibration and Journal of Low Frequency Noise, Vibration and Active Control, and a Guest Editor of IEEE TRANSACTIONS ON MECHA-TRONICS, IET Control Theory and Application, IET Intelligent Transportation Systems, Mechatronics, and Advances in Mechanical Engineering.
